IIT students leaving India 
*81.  SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY:† 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that twenty per cent of the lITians are still 
leaving India inspite of globalisation and liberalisation; 
(b) whether Government have any statistics indicating the number 
of lITians who have left India during the last three years, year-wise and 
institution-wise; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to stop this brain-drain? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) No record of the number of lITians leaving the country is 
being maintained centrally. Most of the students go abroad for higher 
studies or employment after completing their under graduate studies.   
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Rama Muni 
Reddy Sirigireddy. 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
(c) While some students passing out from Indian engineering and 
technology institutions including NTs go abroad for higher studies as well 
as employment, many of the students having gone abroad do return to 
India after a certain period and either take up employment in various 
sectors or establish their own industr ies which further creates employment 
opportunities. Several measures have been taken from time to time by 
the Government to minimize the outflow of professionals from various 
fields and also to attract Scientists and technologists settled abroad to 
return to India. Some of these measures are:— 
(i) Setting up of more centres of excellence/advanced studies in 
the universities and academic institutions. 
(ii) Science and Technology based training for entrepreneurial 
development. 
(iii)  Invitation to distinguished men and women of Indian origin settled 
abroad for short term technical assignments to assist in frontier 
and emerging areas of Science and Technology. 
(iv) Increasing the number and amount of fellowships for M. Tech. 
programme as a result of which, more students have started 
joining the M. Tech. programme. 
(v)  Early Faculty Induction Programme which aims at attracting bright 
and young under-graduate students in Engineering and Technology/ 
Pharmacy/Architecture etc. to take teaching as their career. 
(vi) Appointment of NRIs and persons of Indian Origin in the 
permanent faculty positions in the NTs. 
(vii)  NTs have also established Innovation and Incubation Centres which 
encourage students to start their own enterprises after graduation. 
(viii)  Encouraging graduate students to continue work on sponsored 
research projects which have been funded by various agencies. 
(ix)  Conduct of counseling sessions for career options of students 
and taking necessary steps for recruitment of students in Indian 
industries and organizations registered in India. 
However, in the present scenario of globalisation and liberalization, 
movement of technical personnel across the national boundaries is not 
only inevitable but in many cases could give positive benefits to this

NCERT text books in CBSE affiliated schools 
*83. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that NCERT published text books are studied 
exclusively by students in the CBSE affiliated schools; 
(b) the subjects in which NCERT books are exclusively prescribed 
and since when; 
(c) number of times revisions, if any, carried out in the originally 
published books on the respective subjects; 
(d) the procedure laid down and followed in carrying out such 
revisions on each occasion; 
(e) whether NCERT book(s) on any su bject are presently undergoing 
revision; 
8 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) Subjects in which the NCERT books exclusively prescribed are:— 
Classes-IX-X: English Language & L iterature, Hindi Course A, Hindi 
Course B, Urdu Course A, Urdu Course B, Mathematics, Science and 
Technology, Social Sciences. 
Classes-XI-XII: History 
This was implemented with the introduction of the 10+2 scheme in 1975. 
(c) The text books are updated on a regular basis, as per established 
practice. It may be mentioned that although NCERT prepared a few 
textbooks before 1975, it was with the introduction of the 10+2 scheme 
in 1975 that preparation/printing of textbooks for all classes I to XII was 
undertaken by NCERT. 
(d) The NCERT Executive Committee, in its meeting on 9.1.1976, 
laid down the procedure for preparation of manuscripts of textbooks. 
Accordingly, Editorial Boards were constituted for the revision during the 
phase 1975-79. The books were authored by members of the Editorial 
Board, outside experts and members of the NCERT faculty. 
During the second phase, a Central Advisory Board for Science 
and Mathematics, under the Chairmanship of Dr. CNR. Rao, the then 
Scientific Advisor to PM, was constituted and their proposals were 
considered by the Executive Committee in its meeting on 24.12.1986. 
Textbook writing teams, numbering six, with members drawn from internal 
faculty and outside, were formed to develop syllabi and textbooks 
(classes-VI to XII). For Social Sciences/languages (classes-VI to XII), 
the concerned departments of NCERT undertook the work, associating 
faculty as well as the outside experts in developing syllabi and textbooks. 
As far as primary classes are concerned, the concerned 
departments of NCERT, with the help of outside experts, developed the 
syllabi and prepared the textbooks. 
The final drafts of manuscripts were reviewed in workshops.

constituted and the books were authored by teams including members

comprising Professors S. Settar, J.S. Grewal and Barun De. 
The Terms of Reference of the panel were as follows: 
'The issues of communalisation and inadequacies of history textbooks 
of the NCERT have engaged public and academic attention for a long 
time. These text-books have been mostly printed for the current year and 
in a substantial number of schools teaching works has already started, 
based on these books. It is, therefore,  impractical to withdraw these books 
at this st3ge and replace them with mo re appropriate books without causing 
dislocation in the studies of millions of students. However, the same 
impracticability should not result in our  children learning either communal 
views or distorted facts of history. Even as the processes are initiated to 
address the long term remedial measures, including reconstitution of 
Central Advisory Board of Edcuation (CABE) and the initiation of the process 
of curriculum frame-work review, as a short term measure, it has been 
considered necessary to do a quick review of these books by a panel of 
eminent historians of impeccable cred entials, to suggest what needs to be 
done in the short term. If they so recommend, the Government will direct 
the NCERT and the CBSE to issue appr opriate directions to the teachers 
to transact the curriculum as per those recommendations. In particular, 
the recommendations should be for removing distorted and communally 
biased portions and for inclusion of short passages which will fill in the 
gaps that some of these books are supposed to be having or could develop 
after the removal of the aforesaid mentioned passages. The three 
distinguished historians have been requested by the Government to submit 
their recommendations at the earliest so  that the interventions could be 
made, if necessary, as early as possi ble, in the academic session that has 
already started in some schools in the country. Joint Secretary (School 
Education) in the Ministry of Human Resource Development will provide 
secretariat and logistics support to this group." 
The panel has submitted its report. I regret to inform the House that 
the complaints made about the errors and biased nature of the books, 
have been found to be correct by the panel. 
10 
 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Among other things, the report brings out the following: 
* The textbooks prepared since 2 000 are 'so full of errors and 
sub-standard' that the panel finds it impossible to reocmmend 
their continuation. The errors are so many that rectification of 
each one of them is almost impossible. 
* It also states that there is a common strand of bias that runs 
through the entire series. This bias gives more weight to Hindu 
religious practices and revival movements distinguished from 
other religious or modernizing traditions that have been, in the 
last one thousand years, as much, a part of India's composite 
culture as the ones of earlier origin. 
* They, therefore, propose that a lis t of alternative reading material 
viz. books prepared by private publishers may be recommended 
for students of Class VI to X for the current academic year till 
alternative material prepared, th rough due process, is prepared 
by the NCERT in time for the next academic year. 
* The Panel is aware of the fact that alternative material is 
unavailable for classes XI and XI I at present. The three members 
have made suggestions that, ei ther on the existing books or on 
reviving the old books, it would be necessary to issue proper 
advisories to teachers. Whereas,  Prof. Barun De has suggested 
that, the book on 'Modern India' by Bipan Chandra for Class XII 
should be revived, if necessary, by updating it. Prof. Grewal has 
similarly suggested that the book on 'Medieval India' by Satish 
Chandra should be revived with a proper advisory. For the 
'Ancient Period', Prof. Settar has suggested further scouting for 
alternative reading material. 
The findings of the Committee have put the Government in a very 
difficult situation. On the one hand, because the panel has found the 
books to be of unacceptable quality and content, it is not appropriate to 
continue with them. On the other, the academic session has begun quite 
some time back in some schools and it would be unfair to students and 
techers to be asked to use different textbooks at this late stage. Making 
available alternative texts throughout the country will also pose serious 
problems of logistics and cannot be ar ranged in a satisfactory manner till 
very late in the academic session. At the moment, the Govemment is 
trying to address this serious dilemma which has been caused by the

distortion of history books. When the NCFSE was released in November 
2000, it had neither the approval of the Executive Committee nor the 
General Body of the NCERT. It was also not endorsed by the Central 
Advisory Board of Edcuation (CABE). 
The present Government has already constituted the CABE. It seeks 
to ensure that all the processes are duly followed which were undermined 
during the last few years. 
As such, the recommendations of the panel of historians will be put 
up for consideration of the Executive Committee (EC) of the NCERT in 
its meeting on 14 July, 2004. While taking a decision, the EC will no 
doubt keep the interest of students as their foremost concern.

Trade Organisation (WTO) have been meeting in the WTO Committee on 
Agriculture, Special Session, from time to time to negotiate modalities for 
further commitments under the WTO agreement on agriculture. They met 
formally last on 25th June, 2004. The Committee has been working under 
the broader objective of reaching possi ble agreement on agriculture, which 
will then be considered, along with proposals on non-agricultural products 
and other areas included in the Doha  Work Programme, by the General 
Council of WTO at its meeting scheduled for 27th—29th July, 2004.

with other like-minded countries, has been seeking substantial reduction 
in trade-distorting domestic support,  elimination of all forms of export 
subsidies provided by developed countries and substantial market access 
improvements particularly in products of export interest to developing 
countries. Any further commitments  in market access by developing 
countries has to fully take into account their rural development needs 
and food and livelihood security concerns. Special and differential

electronic media in the field of advertis ements is badly affecting the cultural

Government has constituted an In ter-ministerial Committee under 
Section 20 of Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 which is

be able to sustain real GDP growth rates in the range of 6-7% in 2004-2006.

growth is expected to pick up additional momentum in 2004 should the global

Session of the UNCTAD Conference which was held at Sao Paulo, Brazil

between national strategies and the global economic processes towards 
economic growth and development, particularly of developing countries". 
India alongwith other developing countries group known as G-77 and

countries under the multilateral trading system. The developing countries 
succeeded in pointing out that the central issue of the globalisation should

Agreement in WTO 
164. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in a bid to reach an agreement on a negotiating framework 
for key issues like agriculture and non-agriculture, the World Trade 
Organisation General Council Chairman has urged members to work towards 
arriving at a shared understanding of the package as early as possible; 
(b) if so, whether Govenrment have made any efforts with other 
countries to solve agriculture norms/non-agriculture issues in the WTO; and 
(c) if so, to what extent it has succeed ed and by when a final decision 
is likely to be taken by WTO? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) India has been coordinating regularly with the other 
Members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) having similar interests 
and concerns on various issues in the on-going negotiations under the 
Doha Work Programme, including in agriculture. Thus India is part of 
developing country groupings like the G-20 (Agriculture) and G-16 
(Singapore Issues). In respect of al l these issues, incl uding agriculture 
and non-agricultural products' market acc ess, discussions are taking place 
in the various negotiating bodies const ituted in WTO in order to come to 
an understanding on the 'framework' of negotiations. These efforts are 
aimed at achieving a balanced outcome, including special and differential 
treatment for developing countries to enable them to meet their 
developmental and trade concerns. The negotiations are formally 
scheduled to conclude by 1 January, 2005 in accordance with the mandate 
given by the WTO Ministers at Doha in November 2001. At this stage, 
since the negotiations are on-going, it is  difficult to estimate the success 
or otherwise of India's efforts in these negotiations.

(d) The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 provides for the welfare of 
plantation labour and regulates the conditions of work in plantations, 
including tea. This act is administer ed by the State Governments and it 
specifies the various facilities to be provided to the workers. Government 
of India had taken up the matter regarding the problems being faced by 
the workers of the tea gardens with the concerned State Governments for 
intervention and providing necessary relief. Some State Governments like 
West Bengal and Kerala, where the number of closed tea gardens are 
more, have taken steps to provide relief to the affected plantation workers 
and their families. This include creation of employment opportunities through 
various schemes, extending health care, implementing nutritior 
programmes for children, distribution of foodgrains, augmenting drinking 
water facilities and distribution of cash to the most needy. 
(e) and (f) The plantation crops mainly tea and coffee have been 
affected due to the fall in prices dur ing the last few years. A number of 
steps have been taken to help the tea and coffee growers. So far as tea is 
concerned, a package of Special Tea Term Loan (STTL) has been 
announced recently which envisages re structuring/rephasing of outstanding 
term/working capital loans in the tea sector with repayment over 5 to 7 
years and a moratorium of 1 year. The STTL also provides for working 
capital upto Rs. 2 lakhs at a rate not exceeding 9% to small growers. The 
Government has issued orders regarding implementation of a Price Subsidy 
Scheme for small tea growers for a period of four months from February to 
May 2004. Tea Board is also implementing a price sharing formula between 
small tea growers and manufacturers of made tea w.e.f. 1.4.2004. A special 
fund has also been set up out of collections by way of additional duty of 
excise of Re. 1 per kg. on tea for the development, modernisation and 
rehabilitation of tea plantation sector. In order to mitigate the problems of 
coffee growers, Government of India has taken a series of steps which 
include re-phasement/restructuring of loans taken by the coffee growers 
from commercial banks by way of Special Coffee Term Loan (SCTL), 
interest subsidy to small and large coffee growers on the repayment of 
working capital loans taken from financial institutions, reduction in import 
duty on specified machinery for coffee se ctor to 5% to enable the industry 
to improve the quality and productivity of coffee for making it globally 
competitive. Commercial Banks have also agreed to extend crop loans 
upto a maximum of Rs. 50 lakhs at 9% interest so as to benefit the coffee 
gorwers having land holdings upto 60 ha. In addition, the Coffee Board is 
implementing a medium-term export strategy to sustain and gain market 
share in the key markets a nd also to improve the competitiveness of Indian 
coffee in the global markets over the next few years.

with a corpus of Rs. 500 crore for th e benefit of tea, coffee, rubber and

Industrialisation of backward States 
173. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to stat e the details of the schemes and 
programmes formulated and being implemented and the incentives being 
given by Government for the rapid industrialisation of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, 
Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and North Eastern 
Region? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): Promotion of industrial 
development in backward areas is primarily dependent on the initiatives 
of the State Government/Union territories. The Union Government 
supports the State's efforts through various incentive/development 
schemes such as the Growth Ce ntre Scheme, Transport Subsidy 
Scheme, the Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme. For the 
North Eastern States including Sikkim , special incentive packages had 
been notified. The details are as under: 
Fiscal Incentives and Developm ental schemes for All States 
including North Eastern region 
Section 80-IC of the Income-Tax Act provides fiscal incentives to 
certain special category States incl uding the North Eastern States. As 
per this provision a new industrial undertaking set up or after the 24th of 
61 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
December 1997 but before 1.4.2007 or an existing undertaking which 
undertakes substantial expansion during this period and which is located 
in certain notified areas is eligible for 100% income-tax exemption for a 
period of 10 assessment years. A simi lar deduction is available for all 
new undertakings or existing undertakings which undertake substantial 
expansion and which are engaged in specified thrust sector activities. 
Tax incentive are also available to industries set up or before 
31.3.2004 in the backward districts of the country, including in the States 
of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattis garh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and 
Rajasthan. While industries in Category A backward districts are eligible 
for 100% deduction for 5 years followed by 25% (30% in the case of 
companies) for the next 5 years, in dustries in Category B backward 
districts are eligible for 100% deduction for 3 years followed by 25% 
(30% in the case of companies) for the next 5 years. The copy of Ministry 
of Finance's order regarding Category A and B backward districts is given 
in Statement-I (See below). 
Growth Centre Scheme 
With a view to promote industrialisation of the backward areas in the 
country, the Central Government in June, 1988 announced Growth Centre 
Scheme. Under this scheme 71 growth centres have been approved 
throughout the country which would be provided with basic infrastructure 
facilities like power, water, telecomm unication, sewage, effluent disposal 
etc. to enable the States  to attract industries. The growth centres approved 
by the Government of India are to be developed by the State Government 
with Central assistance of Rs. 10 crores  per centre (Rs. 15 crores in the 
case of North Eastern Region including Sikkim and Special category States 
viz.:- Jammu and Kashmir, Uttaranchal and Himachal Pradesh). 
Details of the Growth Centres sanctioned in the States of Uttar 
Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and 
North Eastern region is enclosed in Statement-ll. (See below). 
Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme 
The scheme introduced in 1994, envisages to develop infrastructure 
facilities for small industries to facilitate  location of industries in rural/ 
backward areas. The Central Gove rnment and Small Industries 
Development Bank of India contribute to each IID Centres Rs. 5 crore in 
the ratio of 2:3 and the cost in excess thereof and the cost of land is met 
by the concerned State Government. 
62 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
For the North Eastern States, the funding pattern (sharing of funds) 
has been changed from 2:3 between Government of India and SIDBI/ 
Financial Institutions to 4:1. 
Schemes for the North Eastern Region 
(1) Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme 
Under this Scheme a subsidy @  15% of the investment in plant and 
machinery subject to maximum of Rs. 30 lakh would be admissible to 
eligible industries. 
(2) Central Interest Subsidy Scheme 
The Scheme provides subsidy on interest @3% on the working 
Capital loan for eligible industrial units. 
(3) Comprehensive Insurance Scheme 
This Scheme envisages insurance benefits of 100% premium to all 
eligible industrial units. 
(4) Transport Subsidy Scheme 
The Scheme was introduced in July, 1971 to promote industries in 
hilly, remote and inaccessible areas.  Under the Scheme subsidy ranging 
from 50%-90% is admissible on transport costs incurred on movement 
of raw materials and finished goods from designated rail heads/ports up 
to the location of the industrial units and vice-versa for a period of five 
years from the date of commencement of commercial production. The 
scheme is valid up to 31.3.2007. 
The Development Commissioner (Small Scale Industries), Ministry 
of Small Scale Industries is al so implementing various Schemes/ 
Programmes for the benefits of SSI sector in addition to Integrated 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (IIDS) uniformly throughout the 
country. Some of them are as under:- 
1. Tool Rooms provide training facilities in the field of tool design, 
dye making etc. 
2. Central Footwear Training Institutes impart training on shoe design 
and related matters through CAD/CAM. 
3. Process-cum product Development Centres at Meerut, Agra and 
Kanauj provides training and undertake product development. 
4. Under Integrated Technology Upgradation and Management 
Programme, clusters of small-scale in dustries are taken up for technology 
upgradation and other overall development. 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
5. ISO-9000/14001 Certification Reimbursement Scheme provides 
reimbursement upto Rs. 75,000/- or 75% of the cost, whichever is more 
incurred by the units for obtaining requisite certification from the competent 
authority. 
6. Regional Testing Centres and Field Testing Stations provide 
testing facilities for BIS Standard of products. 
7. The Marketing Development Assistance Scheme has been 
launched to introduce appropriate packaging and bar coding of products. 
8. Credit Guarantee Trust Fund has been set up to provide guarantee 
for collateral free credit facilities upto Rs. 25 lakhs. 
9. Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme provides 12% of capital 
subsidy (to a maximum of Rs. 4.8 lakhs) for upgradation of technology.

categories i.e., Category 'A' and Category 'B' Section 80-IA was amended

classify the industrially backward districts of Category 'A' and industrially 
backward districts of Category 'B'. The said Ordinance has come into 
force on the 16th September, 1997. Rule 11EA of the Income Tax Rules,

Statement-I 
UPSC Comments 
1. Induction in the CAS through the Civil Services Examination may 
not be able to meet the technical and specialised requirements of the 
various posts in the proposed CAS. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
2. Persons appearing for Civil Services do so with basically the 
Civil Services in mind and CAS by defin ition is different from other Services 
included in the present Civil Services Examination. 
3. Recruitments are also proposed to be made partly through the 
Engineering Services Examination and partly from the Indian Forest 
Service Examination, and this would subsequently be integrated in the 
cadre of Archaeological Service. It may be noted that the educational 
qualifications for Civil Service Examination are entirely different. To 
integrate recruits taken from these th ree different examinations into a 
single Archaeological Service subs equently may lead to various 
administrative constraints. 
 
4. The CAS is envisaged to be a small Cadre and their induction annually 
will be low. It is seen from the Note for Cabinet that the total staff strength of 
the Archaeological Survey of India (Group 'A') is stated to be 166. This in 
itself implies that the cadre strength of  the proposed Archaeological Service 
would be small. As per instructions issued by DOP&T, the direct recruitment 
to any cadre/service in a single year cannot exceed 1 % of the cadre strength. 
In such a scenario, the total intake into the proposed Archaeological Service 
in any year is unlikely to be more than one. This hardly justifies the inclusion 
of Archaeological Service as a part of  the Civil Services Examination or 
holding a separate regular Examination. 
5. The best option for selecting people to the different specialised 
service would be through the process of Recruitment Test to be held not 
necessarily annually but at required intervals depending upon the 
vacancies which arise in different Wings. Through a Recruitment Test, it 
would be ensured that specific educ ational qualifications/experience as 
required for each of the specialised Wings is met with and also that only 
such officers are selected who are interested in joining the service. 
 
6. The Commission has also conducted recruitment test for direct 
recruitment to the post of Meteorologist Grade-ll (scale of pay Rs. 8,000- 
13,500-JTS) in the India Meteorological Department where Recruitment Rules 
provide for different branches in the Service as in CAS and where recruitment 
is not through Examination but through Recruitment Tests/Recruitment. 
7. It may perhaps be feasible to have a Central Archaeological 
Service (CAS). However, it is not worth to include the new Service as a 
part of the Civil Service Examination nor it may be necessary to hold any 
other examination for recruitment to the Service. However, Recruitment 
Tests could be conducted for the purpose.

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA

191. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the private universities in the country, State-wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that UGC ha s decided not to recognize the 
degrees issued by the private universities; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether any guidelines have been issued for maintenance of 
the private universities; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; 
(f) the details of the private universities which are following the 
guidelines; State-wise; and 
(g) the details of the private universities which are not complying 
with the guidelines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a)to(g) 
According to the information furnished by the University Grants Commission 
(UGC), 113 private universities have been established by some of the States 
in the country is given in the Statement (See below). The private universities 
are required to adhere to the provisions of the University Grants Commission 
(Establishment and Maintenance of Standards in Self-Financing Private 
Universities) Regulations, 2003. These regulations lay down the norms for 
the establishment and maintenance of standards in a private university 
which, inter alia, includes setting up of a private university, opening the off 
campus centres etc. by private unive rsity, minimum criteria in terms of 
programmes, faculty, infrastructural facilities, financial viability and the 
consequences of violations of the laid down norms. The UGC is in the 
process of conducting inspections of these private universities to verify 
their conformity with these regulations.

Opening of more IITs 
192. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to open some 
more IITs; 
(b) if so, the States where these IITs would be set up; 
(c) whether any feasibility study has been carried out in those 
States; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(d) Yes, Sir In view of the announ cement made by the Prime Minister 
on 15th August, 2003 that five new NTs will be set up by upgrading 
promising academic institutions, the Government has constituted an 
Expert Committee to identify such academic institutions. A number of 
proposals from various State Governments have been received by the 
Government and are under considera tion of the Expert Committee. The 
Report of the Committee is awaited. 
Directives on fee formula for IIMs 
193. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government had thoroughly gone to the cases relating 
to the decision to reduce fees of IIM by the previous Government; 
(b) if so, whether he had convened meeting of all IIMs Directors in 
the month of June, 2004; 
(c) if so, the new directive issued to them and whether Government 
have finalised a compromise formula for IIMs fee; and 
100 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, to what extent this has been acceptable to all the IIMs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. All ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(d) The Government reduced the fee for the post-graduate programmes 
(PGP) in Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) to Rs. 30,000/- per 
annum vide orders dated 5th February, 2004. The issue of reduction of 
fees of IIMs was brought to the attention of present Government 
immediately after its assumption in office. 
The meetings of all Chairman and Directors of IIMs were convened 
on 31st May, 2004 and 29th June, 2004 to discuss the reduction of fee 
issue. At the instance of the Government, all the six Indian Institutes of 
Management (IIMs) at Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Calcutta, Lucknow, Indore 
and Kozhikode have decided that: 
(i) The Institutes will ensure that  no student faces any difficulty in 
pursuing education for PGP at the Institute for want of financial resources, 
(ii) The fees charged by the Institutes in the year 2003-2004 will be 
continued in the session starting in June, 2004; 
(iii) All the IIMs will provide a need-based financial assistance 
scheme to both the first and second year students; 
(iv) All students admitted, whose annual gross family income is Rs. 
2 lakh and below, will be eligible for financial assistance up to a full tution 
fee waiver; and 
(v) The IIMs will consider, in appropriate cases, supporting the 
students beyond the tuition fee waiver. Apart from the tuition fee, the 
expenditure by students on hostel and mess charges can also be waived. 
The IIMs are empowered to take all the decisions regarding fee 
structure. The Government has accept ed the said decision and withdrawn 
its orders dated 5th February, 2004 reducing the fees to Rs. 30,000/- 
vide orders dated 29th June, 2004. 
Paper leakage of All India pre-medical examination 
194. SHRIMATI JAMANADEVI BARUPAL: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had to announce new 
dates for all India pre-medical examination because of the leakage 
of paper earlier; 
(b) if so, whether a number of arrests have been made which 
have shown that there is a gang operating in the country which is 
responsible for such leakages; 
(c) if so, whether such leakages had been reported earlier also; 
(d) if so, what are the steps Government propose to take to see 
that such leakages do not occur in future which affects students; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) Yes 
Sir. 
(b) The Delhi Police arrested six culprits including allegedly the 
kingpin, and the Chargesheet has been filed. 
(c) There was also alleged leakage of question paper of 2003 pre- 
medical examination conducted by CBSE. It is now confirmed and CBI 
has filed a chargesheet in this case against five accused. 
(d) and (e) A high level committee under the chairmanship of 
Dr. J. Veera Raghavan, Former Secretary, MHRD, Government of India 
has been constituted by the CBSE to examine various proceduce 
currently adopted by CBSE which a purpose to identify the loopholes in 
the system of examinations. It will also suggest necessary measures 
for strengthening the system to eliminate any possibility of leakage of 
question papers. 
World Bank assistance for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
195. SHRIMATI JAMANADEVI BARUPAL: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
102 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether World Bank has signed an agreement with India for 
providing assistance of $ 500 million for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan project 
which is aimed at providing education for all the children in the age group 
of 6-14 years by the year 2010; 
(b) if so, the amount and the States where it is to be spent during 
2004-05; 
(c) whether the expenditure for four years period from 2004-05 to 
2007-08 would be around $ 3.5 billion or (Rs. 15750 crore); 
(d) whether it is supported by the grants from DFID and from 
European Commission; and 
(e) to what extent the Central and the State Governments are 
providing resources to implement this plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT(SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(e) Yes, Sir. The World Bank (WB), European Commission (EC) and 
Department of International Development (DFID) of United Kingdom have 
agreed to fund Sarva Shiksha Abhi yan as an ongoing programme. The 
total amount of funding committed is around 1 billion do llars (Rs. 4700 
crores) of which 500 million dollars (around Rs. 2250 crores) is from 
WB, 190 million pounds (1550 crores) from DFID and 160 million Euros 
(around Rs. 900 crores) from EC against an estimated total investment 
of Rs. 15,746 crores during the period from 2003-04 to 2006-07. SSA is 
being implemented in all States/UTs except Goa. The fund sharing pattern 
between the Central and the State for S.S.A. is in the ratio of 75:25 for 
the Xth Plan period.

196. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of  the recent reports ir the issue 
of "Foreign investment in elementary education" as appeared in the print 
media on 25th June, 2004. 
 103

(b) if so, the details including the decisions taken and policy evolved 
or to be evolved; 
(c) the amount of fund allotted and spent for elementary 
education for the last three years, year-wise, State-wise and category- 
wise; and 
(d) the action taken, if any, to grant more funds and facilities to 
elementary education, in details? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(b) Various newspapers reported on 25th June about an interview given 
by Union HRD Minister to a T.V. channel wherein he had said that foreign 
investment in elementary education would be welcome if incorporated in 
a properly formulated policy. He had al so said that at present, there is no 
policy and that the policy has first to be formulated. 
(c) Year-wise, State-wise and Scheme-wise information has been 
given in Statement I, II and III. (See below) 
(d) Plan allocations for Elementary  Education have been steadily 
increasing over the years. In addition, limited external assistance, as and 
when necessay, has been tapped for the universalisation of elementary 
education through the District Prim ary Education Programme, and more 
recently, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. 
State Governments have also been requested to mobilize 
resources from the community, on a voluntary basis, for improvement 
of primary education. 
In the Union budget presented on 8.07.2004, an education cess 
has also been proposed on income tax, corporation tax, excise and 
customs duties, and service tax to fulfil the Government's commitment 
to provide and finance universalized quality basic education.

(b) whether Government, Semi-Gov ernment and Private Sector 
institutions had refused to accept the fee structure proposed by 
Government; and 
(c) if so, the initiatives taken by Government for safeguarding 
interests of the meritorious poor students and implementing instructions 
of the Hon'ble Supreme Court so th at the teaching standards of such 
institutions could be maintained and interest of the poor students could 
be taken careof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to 
(c) The Government had decided vide orders dated 5th February, 2004 
that the fees for the Post-Graduat e Programmes (PGP) in the Indian 
Institutes of Management (IIMs) be fixed at Rs. 30,000/- per annum from 
the academic session 2004-05 and that no other charges/fees should be 
levied from the students except for mess charges that would be payable 
by the students separately. The said orders were not applicable for Semi-

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
At the instance of the Government, all the six Indian institutes of 
management (IIMs) at Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Kolkata, Lucknow, Indore 
and Kozhikode have decided that: 
(i) The Institutes will ensure that no student faces any difficulty in 
pursuing education at the Institute for want of financial resources; 
(ii) The fees charged by the Institutes in the year 2003-04 will be 
continued in the session starting June, 2004; 
(iii) All the IIMs will provide a need-based financial assistance 
scheme to both the first and second year students; 
(iv) All students admitted, whose annual gross family income is Rs. 
2 lakh and below, will be eligible for receiving financial assistance 
amounting upto full tuition fee waiver; and 
(v) The IIMs will consider, in appropriate cases, supporting the 
students beyond the tuition fee waiver. Apart from the tuition 
fee, the expenditure by students on hostel and mess charges 
can also be waived. 
The IIMs are empowered to take all the decisions regarding fee 
structure. Thus, they have taken a decision safeguarding interests of the 
meritorious poor students and also ma intaining the teaching standards. 
The Government has accepted the said decision and withdrawn its orders 
dated 5th February, 2004 reducing the fees to Rs. 30,000/-, vide orders 
dated 29th June, 2004.

powers to the Chief Justice of Indi a to deal with erring Judges and

through his own channels and decide to take any action against them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) and (b) The issue of Judicial 
Accountability was discussed at the Conf erence of Chief Justices held in 
1990 and on the basis of the broad consensus emerging out of the 
deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice of the High Court has the competence to received 
complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when he 
receives any he would look into it for fi nding out if it deserves to be closely 
looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires to be examined, 
he shall have facts ascertained in such manner as he considers 
appropriate keeping the nature of allegations in view and if he is of the 
opinion that the matter is such that it should be reported to the Chief 
Justice of India, he shall do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to 
complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and in regard 
to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. On the basis of the facts 
ascertained, the Chief Justice of the High Court or the Supreme Court, as 
the case may be, shall take such appropriate action as may be considered 
proper, keeping the interests of the judiciary as the paramount consideration." 
The complaints received against the Judges of the Supreme Court 
and the High Courts are dealt with in the manner indicated above. The Judges 
Inquiry Act, 1968 specifies the pr ocedure to deal with misconduct/ 
misdemeanour of Judges of the Supreme Court/High Courts but Government 
has no Constitutional competence to order enquiry against them.

(b) if so, the salient features of the proposed policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
and (b) "National Policy on Urban Street Vendors" was formulated by 
Government of India on 2.1.2004. Salient features of the Policy are given

Statement 
Salient Features of the National Policy on Urban Street Vendors 
This Policy aims to ensure that Urban Street Vendors, an important 
segment of the urban population, find recognition for their contribution to society. 
The Policy is conceived as a major initiative for urban poverty alleviation by 
support to dignified livelihood. The basic objectives of the Policy are: 
- To give vendors legal status by amending, enacting, repealing 
and implementing appropriate laws and providing legitimate 
hawking zones in urban development/zoning plans. 
-  To provide facilities for appropriate use of identified space including 
the creation of hawking zones in the urban development/zoning plans.  
-  To eschew imposing numerical  limits on access to public spaces 
by discretionary licenses and instead moving to nominal fee 
based regulation of access, where ma rket forces like price quality 
and demand will determine the number of vendors that can be 
sustained. Such a demand cannot be unlimited. 
- to make Street vendors a special component of the urban 
development/zoning plans by treating them as an integral and 
legitimate part of the urban distribution system. 
- To promote self-compliance amongst Street, vedors. 
- To promote organizations of Street vendors e.g. Unions/ 
Co-operatives/Associations and other forms of organization to 
facilitate their empowerment. 
- To set up participatory mechaisms with representation from 
urban vendors; orgaizations, (Unions/Co-operatives/ 
Associations), Voluntary orgaizations, local authorities, the 
146 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
12.00 Noon 
police, Residents Welfare Asso ciation (RWA) and other for 
orderly conduct of urban vending activities. 
- To take measures for promoting a better future for child vendors 
by making appropriate interventions for their rehabilitation and 
schooling. 
- To facilitate/promote social security (pension, insurance etc.) and 
access to credit for Street vendors through promotion of SHGs/ 
Co-operatives/Federations/Micro-Finance Institutions (MFIs) etc. 
2. The Policy recommends that the Centre and concerned States should 
amend the Police Act and Police Rules/Regulations as are applicable. 
3. The State Governments should also remove the restrictive 
provisions in the Municipal Acts and make street vendors inclusive in the 
city plan/cityscape. Similar action if necessary, would have to be taken 
by the Development Authority for Development Areas. 
4. All State Governments should  ensure that institutional 
arrangements, legislative framew orks and other necessary actions 
achieve conformity with the national Policy for Street Vendors.

Problems of jute growers in the country 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir, my Special 
Mention is concerning the serious distress that has been confronted with 
by the jute growers, particularly in the Eastern region. 
The United Progressive Alliance Government should be 
complemented for planning to effect upward revision of the Minimum 
Support Price of all Kharif crops. There has been no enhancement of the 
MSP of these crops during 2003, howev er unfortunate it may be. This 
year the Commission for Agricultur al Costs and Prices has already 
recommended an average increase of 3.5 per cent for paddy, pulses, 
soyabean, sunflower, etc. This will certainly spell a sense of relief in the 
lives of millions of poor farming community who are, in fact, languishing 
in a horrifying morass of tremendous crisis. The cost of production has 
got increased manifold due to the sy stematic removal of subsidies on 
fertilizers, electricity, etc. The formidable change in the attitude of the 
new Government is quite satisfying. 
But, I am rather distressed to note that there has been no enhancement 
in the MSP for jute. Millions of peasants, particularly in West Bengal, Assam, 
Bihar and Orissa, are jute growers a nd are already in the vortex of 
insurmountable crisis due to lackadaisical approach of the Jute Corporation 
of India and also the undue preference in use of synthetic bags for carrying 
foodgrains, sugar, etc. There must be a complete reversal of the situation 
and, to begin with, the MSP of jute must be significantly enhanced and the 
JCI must be directed to act in time with regard to procurement of jute from 
the real growers. Usually, these poor people are forced to distress sale in the 
absence of proper and timely initiative of the JCI. 
A few millions of poor people can thus be saved from an ominous 
disaster of the present. Thank you. 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I associate myself 
with my colleague because Andhra Pradesh produces substantial quantity 
of jute. So, the MSP for jute should be enhanced so as to help the farmers.

Need for sincere efforts to stop female foeticide in the country 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karna taka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
according to the latest figures of the Census 2001, the child sex ratio at the 
national level has declined from 945 girls per 1,000 boys in 1991 to 927 
girls per 1,000 boys in 2001. The Census has painted a gloomy picture in 
States like Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat in this regard. 
Another shocking revelation of the Census is that there are sixteen districts 
in the country having less than 800 girls per 1,000 boys. Various reasons 
are cited for this trend such as, son preference, neglect of girl child resulting 
in higher mortality, female foeticide and infanticide. Unfortunately, female 
foeticide through pre-birth sex determination is the major cause for the 
decline in number of girls in the country. Ultrasound machines, scanners 
and imaging machines can detect sex of  foetus and magnitude of this 
disastrous business can be assessed from the fact that there are moe 
than 21,600 registered centres conducting prenatal diagnosis. The number 
of unregistered centres conducting such tests is simply unknown. We can 
imagine at what scale this horrifying business of female foeticide is going 
on in the country killing the girls before their birth. The Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act prohibits 
determination and disclosure of sex of the foetus. But violation of law is 
rampant for which serious thought needs to be given. The registered centres 
should be frequently raided by surprise to curb the misuse, and unregistered 
centres should not only be sealed but their machines and properties be 
confiscated and their owners be put behind the bars. The district authorities 
and local police authorities should be deemed to be guilty if sex 
determination is confirmed in their area and stern action be taken against 
them, the Centre should direct all the States to furnish quarterly reports in 
this regard. The Central Government needs to play its role more effectively 
in implementing the law so that the girl child is saved in the country. Thank 
you.

Shocking deaths of infants at Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA (Himachal Pradesh): Sir, through this 
Special Mention, I would like to draw the attention of this House to the 
shocking deaths of innocents at the Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi. The reports 
of deaths of 34 infants in one week, including 12 in a single day, that is, 
on July 3, 2004, ranging from the age of one month to two years at the 
Safdarjung Hospital has shocked the society. The causes of death include 
septicaemia, anaemia, sepsis and intestinal obstruction. Apparently, most 
of these lives were lost for want of adequate medical treatment in this 
prestigious hospital in the nation's capital. The doctors, treating these 
little patients, have blamed shortage of essential medicines, IV fluids and 
non-availability of ventilators as primary causes of these deaths. 
Doctors have gone on record to state that there were major shortages 
of important antibiotics: Monosafe, Magnamycine and Fortum. Parents in 
distress were asked to purchase the same from the market causing critical 
delays. The fact, that the hospital had given a requirement of three ventilators 
in each ward but only six were sanctioned last year and no purchases 
have yet been made, is a stinging indictments of the health system. No 
paediatric ICU and portable x-ray machines are available for the children's 
ward. That these machines have not been functional for the last one year, 
speaks volumes of the criminal neglect on the part of the concerned 
authorities. In the 21 st century India, which is scaling great heights in science 
and technology, the tragic loss of these infants' life is a shameful stigma 
and unpardonable crime on the part of the concerned authrities. The Health 
Ministry must ensure accountability through an impartial probe and punish 
the callous officials. All medicines and attendant facilities must be made 
available to avoid repetition of such deaths.

kindly look into the matter. {Interruptions)

THE VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Mr. 
Shankar Roy Chowdhury, you have ten minutes. 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY (West Bengal): Mr. Vice- 
Chairman, Sir this has been a very welcome Railway Budget because it 
has been welcomed by the people. There has been no increase in fares 
and no increase in freight charges. In that sense, it is a dream-budget; it 
is a people-friendly it is because, at least, by my calculations, going through 
the various figres given to me, there seems to be a vast shortfall in 
resources for all the very good schemes that have been put forward by 
the hon. Railway Minister. But, I would like to touch on a few points only. 
Firstly, I think, the biggest strategic step the Indian Railways have 
taken, right after 1947, is the decision to link Kashmir with the rest of the 
country. It is a major strategic step. But, I think, we seem to have forgotten 
that we have a Kashmir without Railway lines in the North West, and we 
have a complete North-East seven-sister States, with very few Railway 
lines in the East. We have, rightly, perhaps, focussed on Kashmir. This 
has become a national project for which the Railways have got a special 
grant of Rs. 3,500/- crores. They have created another major Railway 
project, which is the pride and envy of  the world, the Konkan Railway, 
costing Rs. 3000/- crores. I think, Mr . Vice-Chairman, Sir, the Railway 
Minister must now focus on the North East. The Railway project in the 
North East must be taken up as a national project, on the same scale as 
the Jammu and Kashmir and the Konkan Projects were taken up. So, a 
special grant has to be made to a national project. I don't know, what the 
figures will come to. For the Jammu and Kashmir project, the grant was 
Rs. 3,500/- crores, and for the Konkan Railway, it was Rs. 3,000/- crores. 
But, here, I don't know what the figures will come to. I think, now a 
comprehensive scheme to link the entir e North East with railway lines 
must be taken up as a national project. And, a very important thing is that 
no industry is going to come up in the North-East unless there is railway 
line of some kind. A very good step has been taken by the Railways in 
Jammu and Kashmir. They have now come on the stretch between 
Udhampur and Kazigund. The major issue is the railway tunnel. It will 
 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [12 July, 2004] 
take a long time. I hope, it gets through in time. But they have air-lifted 
coaches into the Valley to provide inter-city services between Baramulla 
and Kazigund. I think, the Railways must now take an initative to provide, 
at least, inter-city services in the entire North-Eastern Region. 
My second point pertains to the Railways in the 21st century. We 
have got a rail network which is being doubled, strengthened, and 
expanded. But to go into the 21st century, I think, the Indian Railways will 
have to have special high-density, high speed railway corridors for 
passengers as well as goods trains. Now, this existing railway system, 
no matter how much you put into it, I do not think, will survive. You cannot 
run, say, a Burdwan-Katwa Passenger and a Rajdhani Express on the 
same network. The railway lines have got to be different, the rolling stock 
has got to be different, the locomotives have got to be different, and the 
signal system has got to be different. It is a huge project. So, this, at 
least, the Railwas have got to think about and put into operation. 
I would like to refer here, Sir, to a question I had put to the then hon. 
Minister of State for Railways. This was put by me on 2nd May 2003. The 
question was, "Will the Minister of Railways be pleased to state whether 
Government have prepared perspective plans to extend Railways into the 
North-eastern States of Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh 
and Meghalaya. If so, the scope and time-frame of such plans. If not, the 
reasons for not extending rail linkages to the State." I will not go into the 
details of the answer given to me. They only dealt with the existing schemes 
that are being taken there. But the major issue, "does the Government have 
perspective plans to extend Railways into the North-East", the answer is 
silent. I do hope and I urge the Government very strongly to please prepare 
a perspective plan for the entire North-East, because this is one of the most 
neglected, the most backward regions of the country, and, indeed, priority is 
being given to various States. There have been inter-State disputes, when 
Railways were made into smaller divisions, there were inter-State disputes, 
there was no scheme for the North-East Frontier Railway, there were no 
disputes between States because this is a forgotten corner of the country. I 
think, the most important Railway today, and the Railway must pay more 
attention to bringing up in the North-East Frontier Railway. 
I must thank the hon. Railway Mini ster for the various projects he 
has given to the State of West Bengal. And, in this connection, I was very 
happy to learn that in connection with the Sagarmala Project of developing 
the major ports of the country, a container train left the Calcutta station of 
Alipur, which is the station for the Kiderpur docks and proceeded to Nepal, 
212 

[12 July, 2004]                     RAJYA SABHA 
Virganj in Nepal. It was a container train. It is the first of its kind, and, I 
think, the Railways are saying that they will run, I think, the figure is, six 
container trains per month, or, some such figure, I may be corrected. But it 
is a very good step because the big advantage, Calcutta has a port over all 
other ports in the country, is that it is the Northern-most port, not the Eastern- 
most, but the Northern-most port. That means, with the trade route opening 
up to China, instead of going all the way round to the Eastern sea coast of 
China, Western China and the Tibet region can be approached directly 
through Calcutta Port, so, this I think, is a very good step and, I hope, the 
Railways will strengthen the system, at least, as far as the West Bengal is 
concerned. The freight charges have not been increased; it is a good sign. 
But then, my questions about resources remain. 
I was glad to note that CONCOR has started a roll-on - roll-off project 
on the Konkan Railways. I think this must be strengthened and introduced 
into other systems also, particularly, on a future system perhaps, which 
will connect Kolkata northwards, and further across the Nathu-la, as a 
trade route to China. 
Thirdly, Sir, I wish to speak about the Railway Protection Force. Now, 
the Railways are giving extra responsibility to the Railway Protection Force - 
- that is very good. It is mentioned in the hon. Railway Minister's report about 
additional training facilities to be provided to this force. The Railways must 
understand, as I am sure they do, that the Watch and Ward force - the 
Railway Protection Force was basically a Watch and Ward force - is now 
becoming, firstly, a police force and, in times to come, I have no doubt, it will 
have to function as, more or less, a paramilitary force. Reason is this - 
recently you would have heard, in Jammu and Kashmir, where you are trying 
to construct the Baramulla-Qazigund railway line, the militants had attacked 
and abducted a railway engineer who was later murdered. This is going to 
happen more and more as you extend into the frontier areas of the country. 
So, the Railway Protection Force must now be oriented, not merely on police 
work, not merely as a police force, but I think, training has to be stepped up, 
so that in course of time, it can provide protection to railway property, more 
or less as a paramilitary force, in these disturbed regions. 
A large number of concessions have been made; these are very 
good. People going for jobs, people who are not well, persons 
accompanying people with haemophillia - these are excellent social 
projects, and the Railway Minister deserves credit for introducing such 
ideas which were not there earlier. My only fear is, Mr. Vice-Chairman 
Sir, which I must convey through you to the hon Minister of State for

Railways, that wherever such conce ssions are given, certificates are 
required to be produced. In India there is a major cottage industry of 
false certificates, false visas, false question papers! So, I do hope that 
on all these concessions that are coming up, there will be some check to 
ensure that the certificates being produced are genuine. How the Railways 
are going to do it, I do not know. I frankly cannot see an answer to the 
problem, but this problem is likely to come. 
Also, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Railway Minister 
to the fact that during recent interviews for appointments to Railway jobs, 
there were some very ugly scenes, which do our country no credit. I 
learnt that 8000 constables of the Railway Protection Force are to be 
recruited centrally by the Railways. The Railways must ensure that the 
recruitment is uniformly spread throughout the country and it is controlled 
properly, so that these scenes are not repeated. How they would do it, I 
am sure, they will think of it. 
Finally, Sir, though we have not discussed the Address by his 
Excellency, the President of India, there is a paragraph about the Railways, 
paragraph 35, which said, 'The Railways have suffered immensely over 
the past few years with rail safety being a prime casualty." I think, Sir, with 
due respect to our immensely respected president, whom we all know, 
has to read out what is placed before him by the Government, the 
implications of this one sentence are not fair to the succession of the 
Ministers who have done the work, on whose shoulders we all stand; really, 
we all stand on the shoulders of our predecessors. Everything is developing 
gradually. Nor is it fair to the railways, who are doing a yeomen job. 
This is just a comment I wish to make, Sir. J think that was not a 
very fair comment in the President's Address. I think we should accept 
that the Railways are doing a good job; the Railway Ministry is doing a 
good job. But it is a continuous process, and it does no good to us as a 
nation if we try and disparage, even by implication, the work that our 
predecessors have done. Thank you very much.

SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Thank you, Mr. Vice- 
Chairman, Sir. Sir, through you, first of all, I congratulate the hon. Railway 
Minister for presenting a popular Budget for the year 2004-05. Sir, today, 
in the Railways, the question of safety and security is very important. 
First of all, I would like to thank the hon. Railway Minister for his emphasis 
on safety and security, and raising the allocation for bridgeworks to Rs. 
528 crore, compared to Rs. 277 crore allotted in the last Budget. Of 
approximately 2700 bridges that needed to be rehabilitated, works on 
only 1306 bridges have been completed, which means more than half 
remains untouched. I would like to urge the Minister to take up the matter 
on a priority basis and prevent acci dents. Track renewal is another 
important issue that should be given due importance. I welcome the 
Railway Minister's decision to introduce the Anti-collision Device on nearly 
1700 route KM of the North-East Froniter Railway by the year 2004-05.I 
would also request the Minister to  expedite the process and introduce 
this system in all the zones. 
Similary, the passengers' amenity at stations is another thing that 
has been well addressed by the Railway Minister and I appreciate his 
decision to allocate Rs. 215 crore for this purpose which is higher than 
the previous Budget. 
I would also like to draw the Minister's attention to the case of train 
robbery and only recruiting RPF personnel cannot solve this problem. I 
urge him to take every possible step to stop this and ensure free, safe 
and hassle-free journey for the passengers. 
I would also like to draw the attention of the Railway Minister to another 
issue. The New Jalpaiguri-New Bongaigaon via New Cooch Behar main 
line is, in fact, the lifeline of the North-East. I thank hon. Member, Shri 
Shanker Roy Chowdhury, who has emphasised on the North-East railway 
Zone Sir, this main line connecting North-East faces tremendous pressure 
and now the Railway Ministry has decided to introduce a Sampark Kranti 
Express linking Guwahati with Delhi, which is a commendable move. But 
if doubling work is not complete in the New Jalpaiguri-New Bongaigaon 
stretch, everything will futile and would not serve any purpose at all. So I 
request the Minister to look into the matter and complete doubling work 
from New Jalpaiguri to New Bongaigaon mainline. 
On the other hand, I appreciate t he Minister's decision to allot 
Rs. 42 crores for the New Maynaguri-Jogighopa railway project, though 
the amount is not sufficient. The total project cost is now Rs. 887 crores.

No Railway Minister has even thought of doing this. In fact, there are 
areas in politics where we disagree. But Laluji will go down in India's 
history as a person who climbed from the lower strata of life and his 
responses are always for the poor people. He is, therefore, known among 
the poor people as their saviour. Marginal disagreements in politics will 
continue to be there. Health insurance to vendors and others is a very 
good feature of the Railway Budget. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, jobless candidates can now travel freely for 
examinations and interviews. Some people had stated in the Press that 
they were already travelling without tickets and he was just legalising it. 
It is better to see that they are not committing a crime. Maybe, they were 
doing so because of poverty. No sensible person or a person who can 
afford a ticket will travel without a ticket. But, maybe, because of poverty 
they were doing so. Now, they will travel as honoured citizens of India. It 
is a very good thing. So, he deserves congratulations for this gesture. 
230 

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Now, after giving so many concessions, without charging any extra 
money on freight or without increasi ng the passenger fares, there is a 
surplus of Rs. 873 crores in the Railway Budget. The surplus is not always 
representative of the health of a particular sector. But, even after allowing 
all these concessions, he is not short of money. He has created a surplus. 
We join him in creating a kind of good atmosphere and providing service 
to the nation. After providing all these concessions, he is telling us that he 
will have a surplus. The surplus is not ultimately needed. It must be spent 
on the welfare of the people. We don't need surplus for the sake of surplus. 
Let the Railways grow to eminence. Mr. Gill was paying tributes to our 
engineers and technical staff. Yes, they are one of the most brilliant people 
in the world. India is helping other countries in laying railway tracks. 
Therefore, we want the Railways to grow. It is the greatest employer of the 
nation and more than 16 lakh people are working there. After these good 
features for which I congratulate the Railway Minister, I want to say a couple 
of things about the State of Jammu and Kashmir. When I saw my colleagues 
from Kerala staging a dharna outside, I took some interest. Their grouse 
was that no new train has been proposed for Kerala. With that 'K', I 
remembered my 'K', i.e. Kashmir— from Kerala to Kashmir, from 
Kanyakumari to Kashmir. Jammu and Kashmir deserves special attention 
which is not there, although the Budget says so. That is also a legacy. I had 
joined issue with his predecessor, Shri Nitishji, in this House that what he 
was saying to the House was not correct. He was not taking the House into 
confidence. He was acutally misleading the House. He rose for ten minutes 
to answer my question. I said at that time—record is there—that whatever 
he said about Jammu and Kashmir was wrong. He had given wrong 
information. Shri Nitish Kumar said at that time that by 2007 they would 
take a train to Kashmir. I said that it was not correct at all. The Department 
of Raiiways has not been able to take a train from Jammu to Udhampur in 
27 years! Out of these 27 years, for 22 years I have been in Delhi either in 
this House or in that House. Every time, promises were made that so 
many bridges and so many tunnels would be constructed. But no train has 
gone to Udhampur. When I was Minister, I played my role during Shri Deve 
Gowda's time and during Shri I.K. Gu jral's time. They went and laid a 
foundation stone for a train between Udhampur and Kazigund. Then Shri 
I.K. Gujaral went to Kazigund and Baramulla to lay a foundation stone for 
a train from Kazigund to Baramulla. But it did not happen. Last year, when 
Shri Nitish Kumar provided Rs. 400 crores, I asked, "What are you doing?" 
Then he said that they would take a train to Kashmir in 2007.1 had begged 
of him—at that time he was on this side of the House—I told him to take

the House into confidence and give more money for the section between 
Jammu and Udhampur. I asked, "Why do you say or assert in the House 
that you will take a train to Kashmir by 2007?" I said, "You can never do

Now the Department of Railways has said that they will go to the

get Rs. 20,000 crores, you give Rs. 4,500 crores or whatever be needed

the pattern of Konkan, you creat a Kashmir Railway Corporation or

corporation. Within the Railway Budget, every year you will allot Rs. 400

say, "We shall take a train to Kashmir". It will never come up. There will 
be price escalation. I have yet to look into the Railway Budget minutely 
as to how much money was spent in Jammu and Kashmir last year and 
how much is remaining. I can say that they have built some bridges; they

His predecessor said that Kashmir would be on the Railway Map. I also 
want Kashmir to be on the Railway Map because it would have 
socialisation effect; it would have an effect towards national integration. 
Imagine, 20,000 people from Jammu and Kashmir coming to Delhi and 
going back in the evening. That would have a very good effect. We are 
an integral part of India. We must have all facilities that are available to 
other parts of India. Sir, a rail has not still gone to Kashmir. It is not going

[12 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
The other thing about Jammu and Kashmir that I want to say is this. 
Laluji has proposed that he will create 8,000 jobs. I would say that the 
previous Government applied a moratorium on jobs everywhere perhaps 
in the country, and we have been struggling to put off that Memorandum 
of Understanding signed by the previous Chief Minister. So, Jammu and 
Kashmir has suffered a great deal. This  is a sensitive State, a border 
State, and we must not give youth any chance to get into the net of 
terrorism. We must fight terrorism not just through bullets; we must fight 
terrorism with whatever means we have at our command. Our Army and 
paramilitary forces are doing a very good job. And, in some measure, 
infiltration is countinuing. But the Army and paramilitary forces are alert. 
It will be fought and cross-border insurgency will be fought with great 
vigour. I am sure on that. But there are other means to fight terrorism.

unemployment had been one reason as to why youth took to terrorism in 
a big way. But, now, the number of Kashmiri youth taking to terrorism has

is, out of 100 youths, 10 boys are from Kashmir. So, this is dwindling and

Minister that a sizeable chunk of these jobs must be given to the State of

of the Recruitment Board that t hey have for Jammu and Kashmir has 
invariably been a person from the rest of the country. I raise a demand

Committee that selects youth from Jammu and Kashmir for the jobs must 
be from Jammu and Kashmir. Whatever li ttle jobs that are available, it 
has invariably been a person from outside Jammu and Kashmir. So, 
through you, Sir, I pass on this suggestion to the Railway Minister: Firstly,

in Jammu and Kashmir from Orissa or from Tamil Nadu. It applies vice-
